paras: The threatened lynching of John J. Farris occurred on the night of April 19, 1888, when a crowd gathered at Lewistown, Illinois, intending to take Farris from the Fulton County jail and hang him for the murder of Stephen McGehee. Finding the jail under armed guard, the crowd withdrew, and Sheriff Smith drove the prisoner overnight to Cuba and took him by train to the jail at Peoria. Farris was later tried at Peoria on a change of venue and sentenced to hang.

On April 18, 1888, Farris, the divorced husband of McGehee's wife, entered the McGehee house about three miles south of Canton during dinner and shot McGehee twice, killing him, according to the Canton Register and a Canton dispatch. Mrs. McGehee testified at the inquest that Farris then held her at pistol point, sent the children to the barn and forced her into an old log house, and the papers reported that he "outraged" her. Constable Wilson arrested Farris near Canton that afternoon, and he was taken on the evening train to the county jail at Lewistown.

The coroner's jury, sitting at Canton on April 19, found that Farris had committed willful murder without provocation. The Register wrote that feeling at the inquest was "intense" and that Farris would have been hanged had he been within reach.

Threats of lynching followed, and the sheriff, warned to expect a lynching party, placed a guard at the jail. According to the Canton dispatch, about seventy-five masked men from south of Canton marched that night to Lewistown "for the purpose of executing summary justice." A runner sent to look over the jail reported a heavy guard armed with Winchester rifles, and the party went away. The Register described the crowd only as people from Buckheart and Liverpool, joined by a few from Canton, who gathered at Lewistown Thursday night, and said the contemplated lynching "was not attempted."

During the night Sheriff Smith drove Farris across country to Cuba, where the Register's Cuba column noted he spent part of Thursday night and Friday morning "fleeing to Peoria" from "a lynching party." From Cuba the sheriff took the early Friday train and lodged Farris in the Peoria jail.

No report of arrests of anyone in the lynching party appears in the coverage. The state's attorney sought an early special term, as the Register judged it "exceedingly venturesome" to return Farris to the Lewistown jail until August, and the case was moved to Peoria on a change of venue. Farris's trial opened in the Peoria circuit court before Judge Shaw in December, and on December 22 the jury found him guilty and fixed the penalty at death by hanging. Farris was reported to deny the outrage and to claim he fired before McGehee could "get the drop" on him.

The fullest account of the threat came from a Canton dispatch in the Rock Island Argus, headlined "Guards and Their Guns Stave Off a Lynching That Was Almost Desirable." It called Farris a "devil in human form," attributed the mob's retreat to "the lack of a leader of nerve," and predicted he would "surely be lynched" if brought back to the county. The Canton Register was equally harsh toward Farris, calling him a "brute" and a "fiend," but wrote that it was to the honor of Fulton County that no lynching was attempted and said the sheriff acted "wisely."

Beyond Illinois, short wire briefs on the killing ran in the Wheeling Register, the Indiana State Sentinel and the Perrysburg Journal without mention of the lynching threat. When Farris was sentenced, the Indianapolis Journal recalled that he "was threatened with mob violence," and the Register wrote that the county "well may rejoice" that the change of venue had been taken.

The Argus put the inquest on Friday afternoon, but its own timeline has Farris on the Peoria train early Friday, while the Register's dated coroner's verdict and same-day report place the inquest on Thursday, April 19. The two accounts also differ on the crowd: the Argus describes about seventy-five masked men who scouted the jail, while the Register gives no number or masks and says only that a crowd gathered.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of John J. Farris
bases: A crowd gathered or marched on the Lewistown jail to lynch the jailed Farris and withdrew; he was removed to Peoria and no one was harmed (A3, A6, A7).

No one was killed: the masked party turned back from the guarded Lewistown jail and Farris was taken to Peoria, later tried and sentenced to hang (A3, A6, A11). The party of about 75 sought 'summary justice' for an accused murderer, so it was a threatened lynching only (A3).

The Canton dispatch in the Rock Island Argus and the Canton Register's own reports independently describe a lynching party at Lewistown and the sheriff's flight with Farris via Cuba to Peoria, and a December wire repeats that he was threatened with mob violence (A3, A6, A7, A11).

accounts.label: Canton wire dispatch (Rock Island Argus)
accounts.gist: About seventy-five masked men marched on Lewistown to execute 'summary justice', scouted the jail, found a heavy Winchester-armed guard and went away; the sheriff then slipped off with Farris to Cuba and Peoria.

accounts.label: Canton Register (local weekly)
accounts.gist: A crowd from Buckheart and Liverpool, with a few from Canton, gathered at Lewistown Thursday night, but the contemplated lynching was 'not attempted'; the sheriff, warned in advance, drove the prisoner to Cuba for the early train to Peoria.

accounts.label: December wire (Indianapolis Journal)
accounts.gist: In reporting the death sentence, recalled that Farris had been threatened with mob violence and brought to Peoria for safe-keeping.

framing.detail: The Argus headline 'Guards and Their Guns Stave Off a Lynching That Was Almost Desirable' called Farris a 'devil in human form' and blamed the retreat on 'the lack of a leader of nerve'.

The Canton Register called Farris a 'brute' and 'fiend' but recorded it 'to the honor of Fulton County' that the lynching was not attempted, praised the sheriff as acting 'wisely', and later welcomed the legal death sentence.
Out-of-state papers ran short wire briefs on the killing without the lynching threat, and the Indianapolis Journal's December item mentioned the threat only in passing.
